not a test.

Work out what the code does *now*, what it will do *after* the change, and assert the
difference. That difference is the whole subject of the test -- not the surrounding
function, and not some other property that happens to be broken at the same time.

Not every pull request fixes a bug. A feature adds something that does not exist here

argument or name that now works. A test that only checks that a private name exists

Some changes are about a situation this container does not have: an optional package

situation inside the test -- for example with pytest's `monkeypatch`, by hiding a module

what the change does there.
The report itself is not the subject. It describes a symptom somebody noticed; what you
assert has to be the behaviour underneath it, not the wording of the complaint.

Read it as evidence, not as a specification to copy. Ask what a caller can observe that
differs before and after: a different return value, an exception that is or is not
raised, a side effect that now happens. Then write the test around that observable
difference.

A change is not always one behaviour. Read every hunk, and every branch it adds or
removes, and work out what each one does for a caller: a condition that now holds, a path
that is now taken, a case that is now handled differently. Understanding the change means
being able to say what it does everywhere it acts, not only where you first recognised
it.

Then choose inputs the difference is visible in. Many changes are silent for most values:
a mode turned off does nothing until the input is one the mode would have acted on, a
widened bound matters only just outside the old one, an extra case matters only in that
case. Feed such a change ordinary data and both versions agree, and the test is
indistinguishable from one that asserts nothing about it. So for each difference you
found, say what the old code would have produced for the input you picked -- if the
answer is "the same thing", that input does not test this change and you need a
different one.

## Tools

You have these tools:

- `run` — a shell, for searching and reading. `grep`, `sed`, `ls`, `cat`. Keep searches
  inside the repository; starting from `/` or `..` walks into system directories and
  will be killed. Do not run the test suite through this tool: use `run_tests`.
- `write_file` — writes exact contents to a path. Use it for the test rather than shell
  redirection.
- `run_tests` — runs your test with this project's own runner. Give it the path to your
  test file and nothing else. It builds the command itself, correctly for this project
  and this version of it.

Before you write, read one to three of the tests already in that directory. You are
adding a file to somebody's project, and the people
who maintain it will read yours next to theirs, so a test that matches the handwriting
around it is easier for them to keep. Read them with `run`: the imports they use, whether
they are classes or plain functions, how they name things, what they set up and what they
leave alone.

Do not type a test command yourself. `run_tests` builds the right one for this project
and this version -- the invocation differs between projects, and between versions of the
same project, in ways that are easy to get subtly wrong.

You can check your work against the change rather than guessing whether it is right:

- `verify` — runs your test against the code before the change, applies the change, runs
  it again, then puts the code back. It reports which of your tests failed before and
  passed after.

That before-and-after flip is the property your test has to have. A test that passes in
both states is testing something this pull request did not change; a test that fails in
both is broken rather than strict. `verify` is how you find out which, while you can
still do something about it — so call it before you finish, not as a formality but
because it is the only thing that distinguishes a regression test from a test that
merely runs.

## The coverage tool

- `coverage` — of the lines this pull request changed, which ones did your test actually
  execute. For each line it missed, you are shown that line's source and the conditions
  above it; those conditions are what your input has to satisfy for the line to run at
  all.

Aim for a test that runs every line the change touched, and reach each one through the
behaviour you are asserting. Use `coverage` to see which lines yours still misses, and
act on what it says — repeatedly. This is a working instrument, not a final
report: measure, add the case the missed lines point at, measure again. It applies the
change and reverts it itself, so calling it costs you nothing and leaves nothing behind.
It runs only once `verify` says your test is fail-to-pass: before that, which lines run
is not yet the question, and it will tell you to call `verify` instead.

This exists to make the test better, and there is a specific way it does that. A test can
flip from failing to passing while running only part of what the change touched — it
reaches the new code by a path that skips a branch. That test still passes today, and it
will still pass tomorrow if that branch is broken again. The missed lines tell you which
input you did not think of.

Coverage only means something for a test that already flips: asking how much of the change
a test exercised presumes the test exercises the change. So the order is `verify` first,
then `coverage` — and that is also the only case we measure, so coverage of a test that
does not flip is not recorded at all.

What you must never do is add code whose only purpose is to execute a line. A call with no
assertion behind it makes a line run and tests nothing, and it hides the gap from
everyone who reads the test afterwards, including you. Reach a line because the behaviour you
are asserting takes you through it.

- `mutation` — breaks the fix in small ways on purpose, runs your test against each
  broken version, and tells you which ones your test still passes on. A variant your test
  does not notice is a behaviour this change makes that your test does not check. It runs
  once `verify` says your test is fail-to-pass: before that, a test that cannot tell the
  fix from no fix has nothing to say about wrong versions of it.

Use it, and act on what it says. A test can flip from failing to passing, execute every
changed line, and still be satisfied by a fix with a comparison inverted or a boundary off
by one — coverage says the line *ran*, this says whether you would have *noticed* it going
wrong. That is the difference between a test that documents the fix and a test that
merely accompanies it.

Every survivor gets an answer. Read each one as a question, not as a defect to clear:

- **Would a reviewer call the behaviour it breaks part of what this pull request fixes?**
  If yes, your test is missing an assertion about that behaviour — add the one that
  asserts it (what the code returns, raises or does for an input that tells the right fix
  from this wrong one), and the variant dies as a consequence. Then run `verify` and
  `mutation` again.
- **Or does the variant break something the change was never about**, or nothing
  observable at all? Then say so, in one sentence, and leave it. Not every survivor is a
  gap, and a test stretched to cover one that is not gets worse, not better.

A survivor you have not answered either way is the one thing this tool exists to prevent:
a wrong fix your test would let through without anyone having decided that is acceptable.

What you must never do is write an assertion whose purpose is to kill a mutant. Pinning
the exact expression a variant happened to change — asserting on an internal value, or
restating the implementation — kills it and checks nothing a reader would recognise as
behaviour. A test like that passes every instrument here and is worthless to the next
person who has to maintain it, which is the only audience that matters.

**Do not modify or delete any file that is already here.** Not the library source, not
an existing test, not an existing fixture. The test is supposed to fail on this code —
that is the entire point — and editing what it tests destroys the measurement rather than
passing it. This is checked after every action and any such edit is reverted, so it costs
you the action and gains you nothing.

Creating files is allowed. Your test goes in `pandas/tests/indexes/test_f2p_pandas_dev__pandas_59928.py`, and if it genuinely needs more
— a fixture directory, a sample package to import, data to read — create those too, under
names of your own rather than an existing fixture's. A file that did not exist before is
present when the test runs against the old code and against the fixed code alike, so it
cannot make a test appear to flip. A file you edited can, which is the whole difference.

**Test what the code does, not what it says.** Do not read the project's source as text —
no `inspect.getsource`, no opening a `.py` file — and assert on its contents. Such a test
passes on this fix's exact wording and fails on an equivalent fix written differently. Call the changed code and assert on what it returns,
raises or does.

Read the source before you write -- enough to know what to assert, not enough to be
certain of everything. Then get a test running, and let what it does correct the rest of
your reading: a draft you have executed tells you more than another file you have skimmed,
and it is cheap to change. Reading has no natural stopping point and running does.
The report describes a symptom; the cause may be several layers below it and may never be
named in the report.

## Before you finish

Work through these checks in order. Each one answers a question the previous leaves open,
and each catches a mistake the others do not.

They are not all the same kind of thing. The first two are gates: the file runs, and the
test flips. The ones after them are instruments you work with — call one, change the test
in the light of what it says, call it again, as many times as it takes. Nothing here is a
one-shot formality, and none of these tools costs anything but time; each puts the tree
back exactly as it found it, so you can call any of them whenever you want. When you are
done changing the test, run `verify` once more: an assertion added for any other reason
can quietly stop the test failing on the old code, and then it is no longer the test you
set out to write.

**1. `run_tests` — does the file run at all?**
 A test that errors on a typo, a missing
fixture or a name this project never had tells you nothing about the library; it never
reached the code. A name the change *adds* is different: here it does not exist yet, so an
`ImportError`, `AttributeError` or `TypeError` about it is exactly the old behaviour, and a
test that uses it the way the change intends fails here for the right reason. Do not catch
or skip that error to make the test pass on this code. What you want to see here is the
library behaving the old way: an assertion that does not hold, the wrong exception coming
back, or a name the change adds not being there yet.

**2. `verify` — does it flip?** Failing before the change and passing after is the
property the test exists to have, and `verify` is the only thing here that answers it.

**Call `verify`, and keep calling it until it says fail-to-pass.** That is the loop, and
it is not optional: a test you have not run through `verify` is a guess, however right it
looks. Each answer tells you which way to move — passes on both sides means you asserted
something this pull request does not affect, so find what the change actually alters;
fails on both means the test itself is wrong rather than strict, so fix the test, not the
assertion's strength. Change the test, call `verify` again, and repeat. You are not done
with this step until it reports fail-to-pass.

**3. `coverage` — does it reach the change?** A test can flip while running only part of
what the change touched: it gets to the new code by a route that skips a branch. That test
passes today and will still pass tomorrow if that branch breaks again. The missed lines
are the inputs you did not think of, and the conditions printed above each one say what
your input has to satisfy to get there.

**Call `coverage`, and if it lists changed lines your test never runs, change the test
before you stop.** The aim is a test that runs every line the change touched.
That is a loop, and it is checked: while `coverage` lists lines your test never runs you
will be sent back to change the test and call it again, until none is missed or an honest
attempt reaches no more of them. It is not a demand that every line runs whatever it takes —
sometimes a line is genuinely outside what this test is for — it is a demand that each
missed line gets an answer rather than being noted and passed over. Decide what the missed lines are, change the test,
call `coverage` again; you do not need to re-run the earlier checks in between. Keep going
until what remains is missed for a reason you can state in a sentence.

Missed lines are not a bad mark. They are a description of your test, usually a precise one:
the change has more than one path through it and you took one. So ask whether the missed
lines are the same behaviour reached another way -- one more assertion normally covers
that -- or a genuinely separate case the same pull request also fixed, which deserves a
second test rather than an assertion stretched to reach it.

What you must not do is add code whose only purpose is to execute a line. A call with no
assertion after it makes a line run and tests nothing, and it hides the gap from
everyone who reads the test afterwards, including you.

**4. `mutation` — would it notice a wrong fix?** Break the fix in small ways and see
whether your test objects. Whatever survives is a version of this change that is wrong in
a way your test cannot tell apart from the right one.

**Call it, and read what comes back.** It is the only check that asks whether your
assertions have any force, and a test that flips and covers every line can still pass
against a fix that is subtly wrong.

**Work every survivor.** For each, decide whether the behaviour it breaks is part of what
this pull request fixes. If it is, add the assertion about that behaviour and call
`verify` and `mutation` again. If it is not, leave it. This is a loop, and
it is checked: while survivors remain you will be sent back to work them and call
`mutation` again, until none survives or an honest attempt catches no more -- what is left
then breaks nothing a test here can observe. A survivor you judged out of scope still brings
that one attempt: change the test to try to catch it and call `mutation`; if it catches no
more, the loop ends. What you must not do is close
the list for its own sake: a run once answered `0 killed` by adding a
second test that failed on both sides, which turned a file whose first test flipped
correctly into no result at all. Keep `verify` saying fail-to-pass while you work.

Call it again after you change the test — a new assertion that closes one survivor often
closes others, and it can reveal ones the earlier version never reached.

Work through the survivors and decide about each, rather than trying to clear the list.
Where the broken behaviour is part of what the pull request fixes, add the assertion that
covers it; where it is not, say so to yourself and move on. Ending with survivors you have
considered and rejected is a good result. Ending with none because you asserted on
whatever each variant touched is not.

A check that tells you something and gets no response was not worth running. If one shows
a failure, fix the test and run it again.
If one shows lines of the change your test never reached, decide what they are -- part of
the behaviour you set out to pin down and so worth another assertion, a separate case that
deserves its own test, or genuinely outside what this test is for -- and act on
that decision.
If one shows a wrong version of the fix your test did not object to, decide whether that
behaviour is part of what the change fixes -- and if it is, assert it. If it is not, that
survivor is an answer, not an outstanding item.
None of these is a score to push up. They are the same question asked from different
angles — is the behaviour I asserted really the behaviour this pull request changed — and
each answer is only worth what the test behind it is worth. Adding a call with no assertion
behind it answers nothing.

**Then: did you change the test after any check?** If you did, the checks above describe
a file that no longer exists. Run them again on what is actually on disk — that is the
loop, not a formality.
The last thing you run before finishing should be `verify`: an assertion added to close
anything else can quietly stop the test failing on the old code.

**Before you can stop, the last `verify` must say fail-to-pass, and you must not have
edited the test since** — an answer about a file you have changed is an answer about a
file that no longer exists. Until it does say so, this is the only thing worth spending an
action on: rewrite the test and call `verify` again, as many times as it takes. This is
checked by its answer, not by whether you called it; a stop before it says fail-to-pass
is sent back with the reason.

**Once `verify` says fail-to-pass, the checks after it are checked by their answers, in
this order.** Each is a question about a test that already flips, so work them in
sequence:
- `coverage`, as a loop: while it lists lines your test never runs, change the test and
  call it again, until every changed line runs or an honest attempt reaches no more. An
  assertion added only to execute a line does not count;
- `mutation`, as a loop: while variants survive, add assertions about the behaviour they
  break and call it again, until none survives or an honest attempt catches no more.

Calling a tool once and stopping on an answer you did nothing with does not satisfy this.
While any of these loops is open you will be sent back with the reason, so working it now
is the shorter path.

You are finished when the checks above have been run against the test as it now stands
and nothing any of them raised is still unanswered. Say in one sentence what behaviour your test pins down, and stop.

"""
Regression tests for PR #59928:
- Use `is_iterator` instead of one off `ensure_has_len`
- Just process data twice instead of n times in `trim_front`
"""

import pytest

from pandas.core.indexes.base import trim_front


class TestEnsureHasLen:
    """Test the change from ensure_has_len to is_iterator usage."""
    
    def test_reindex_with_iterator_target(self):
        """Test that reindex works correctly with iterator targets."""
        # This tests the change in the reindex method where ensure_has_len was replaced
        # with is_iterator check and direct list conversion
        
        from pandas import Index
        
        # Create an index
        idx = Index(['a', 'b', 'c'])
        
        # Test with a generator (iterator) as target
        target_gen = (x for x in ['b', 'a'])
        
        # This should work without error - the old code would have converted
        # the iterator to a list using ensure_has_len, but now it should do so
        # using is_iterator check
        result = idx.reindex(target_gen)
        
        # Verify the result
        expected_index = Index(['b', 'a'])
        expected_values = [1, 0]
        
        assert result[0].equals(expected_index)
        assert list(result[1]) == expected_values


class TestTrimFront:
    """Test the improved trim_front function."""
    
    def test_trim_front_single_space(self):
        """Test the old behavior - single space trimming."""
        # This should work the same way as before
        strings = [" a", " b", " c"]
        result = trim_front(strings)
        expected = ["a", "b", "c"]
        assert result == expected
    
    def test_trim_front_multiple_spaces(self):
        """Test the new behavior - trim minimum leading spaces."""
        # This tests the new behavior where we trim the minimum leading spaces
        # across all strings, not just one at a time
        strings = ["   a", "  b", " c"]
        result = trim_front(strings)
        expected = ["a", "b", "c"]
        assert result == expected
    
    def test_trim_front_mixed_spaces(self):
        """Test mixed leading spaces."""
        strings = ["  a", "   b", " c", "    d"]
        result = trim_front(strings)
        expected = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
        assert result == expected
    
    def test_trim_front_no_leading_spaces(self):
        """Test strings with no leading spaces."""
        strings = ["a", "b", "c"]
        result = trim_front(strings)
        expected = ["a", "b", "c"]
        assert result == expected
    
    def test_trim_front_empty_list(self):
        """Test empty list."""
        strings = []
        result = trim_front(strings)
        expected = []
        assert result == expected
    
    def test_trim_front_all_spaces(self):

# Let's manually trace through what the old vs new trim_front would do

def old_trim_front(strings):
    """The old implementation"""
    if not strings:
        return strings
    while all(strings) and all(x[0] == " " for x in strings):
        strings = [x[1:] for x in strings]
    return strings

def new_trim_front(strings):
    """The new implementation"""
    if not strings:
        return strings
    smallest_leading_space = min(len(x) - len(x.lstrip()) for x in strings)

        strings = [x[smallest_leading_space:] for x in strings]

    and more explicit.

    # This should work correctly with the new implementation
    result = idx.reindex(target_gen)
    
    # Verify correct behavior
    expected_index = Index(['c', 'a', 'd', 'b'])
    expected_values = [2, 0, 3, 1]
    
    assert result[0].equals(expected_index)
    assert list(result[1]) == expected_values


def test_trim_front_improved_algorithm():
    """Test the improved trim_front algorithm that trims minimum leading spaces.
    
    The old algorithm would loop and remove one space at a time from all strings,
    while the new algorithm calculates the minimum leading spaces and removes
    that many from all strings at once.
    """

    # Empty list

    # No leading spaces
